exercise1.prompt: Write add(a, b) and subtract(a, b) as a calculator module would, then print 10 + 5 and 10 - 5

cases.name: both functions take two parameters
cases.describe: def add(a, b) and def subtract(a, b)

hiddenCases.name: add works on numbers it was not shown
subtract takes the second number away from the first

exercise1.hint: A module's functions are used by other people, who will pass the arguments in the order your parameters name them. Check which way round subtract takes them.

exercise2.prompt: Write greet(name) returning "Hello, {name}!", then greet "Python" and print the result

cases.name: greet hands the message back rather than printing it

exercise2.hint: A function in a module cannot know what the caller wants done with the answer, so it hands the answer back. Printing and returning are not the same thing.

questions.prompt: What makes a file a module?
choices: A special header at the top
Nothing: any .py file is a module
questions.explain: There is no ceremony. Save functions in greetings.py and import greetings is all it takes.

questions.prompt: You saved functions in greetings.py. How do you import it?
questions.explain: You import the module name, not the filename. The .py is how the file is stored, not what the module is called.

questions.prompt:
# calculator.py holds add(a, b)

___ calculator

print(calculator.___(10, 5))
questions.explain: The module name in front of the function is what says which file the function came from.

questions.prompt: Match each piece to what it is.
right: A call that reaches through the module to the function
questions.explain: The file is the module, the def is a name inside it, and the dot is how you get from one to the other.
